newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean petrol prices to rise after deregulation.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean petrol prices to rise after deregulation.

text.p: Petrol prices at South Korean pumps, already up 12 percent this month, are poised to rise again after January 1 when the government frees up price controls, industry sources said on Tuesday.
Petrol has never been so expensive for South Koreans, who saw prices rise to 815 won (96 cents) a litre earlier this month from 727 won.
It was the highest price rise since 1992 and the first time prices had been above 800 won.
Now, all oil companies, except Hyundai Oil, said they planned to raise prices again -- by as much as two percent. Hyundai, which has the smallest market share, was undecided.
But those leading the price hike move said they wanted to raise prices further but they feared a consumer backlash and government opposition over inflation.

"We'll raise the petrol and other product prices as of January 1 to reflect a rise in crude oil prices and foreign exchange losses," said an official at Yukong Ltd, which holds the largest petrol market share of 38 percent.
Refiners' profits have been hit by a product glut in Asia and foreign exchange losses just as they have embarked on huge capacity expansions, analysts said.
"The petrol price should rise as much as eight percent but we couldn't raise it that much because it would add to consumer burdens and fuel inflation," the Yukong official said.
From January 1, 1997, domestic prices of gasoline, kerosene, diesel and C-type fuel will be deregulated and no longer subject to a government-set monthly price ceiling.
The new regime is part of a wider deregulation of oil product imports and exports, loosening the grip of refineries on the oil trade.
Until the end of June, oil refiners must give the government advance notice of price changes on gasoline, kerosene and diesel. After that, notification after the fact is needed.

But the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said it would intervene if prices became too volatile and endangered the stability of the economy. Refiners found guilty of price fixing or setting prices artificially low to grab market share would be punished according to the Fair Trade Act.
Yukong and Ssangyong Oil Refining Co said they would announce price hikes January 1, and Hanwha Energy the next day.
Petrol prices at LG-Caltex Oil's filling stations will rise to about 830 won ($0.98) per litre as of Wednesday from the 815 won currently, a source close to LG-Caltex said.
Hyundai Oil, the industry's straggler, said it was uncertain but was watching the market cautiously.
"We will wait a couple of days and see what the others do before announcing a price hike," said a Hyundai Oil official.
Analysts said the move might risk spurring inflation but they doubted the government would oppose it.
"The government understands prices have to go up," said Bill Hunsaker, energy analyst at ING-Barings Securities. "It will be very careful not to interfere unless the refiners raise it too much."

Refiners have spent heavily on expansion and need to recoup the costs. But they have also suffered big currency losses. The won has lost about eight percent this year against the dollar, adding to the import cost of crude.

Several analysts estimated the nation's five oil refiners would lose a combined 350 billion won this year against a 8.45 billion shortfall last year. Foreign exchange losses would account for 70 percent of the total.
